recoverable_mathematical_claim.statement: For all real n tending to infinity, the number of primes strictly between n^3 and (n+1)^3 is asymptotic to n^2/log(n).
recoverable_mathematical_claim.assumptions: Unconditional classical analytic inputs as stated by the original Ingham and Huxley papers; no RH.
recoverable_mathematical_claim.domain: As n→∞ through positive real values; no explicit onset or computable constant asserted.
recoverable_mathematical_claim.conclusion: The quantitative count follows from the full short-interval prime-number asymptotic, not merely from a prime-gap upper bound.

auditable_derivation: For alpha in [1/2,3/4], 3/(2-alpha)<=12/5 and log(T)^5<=log(T)^9 for T>=e.
For alpha in [3/4,1], alpha^2+alpha-1>0 and 12*(alpha^2+alpha-1)-5*(5*alpha-3)=(4*alpha-3)*(3*alpha-1)>=0. Thus the exponent coefficient is at most12/5.
The two uniform Huxley branches therefore give N_H(alpha,T)=O(T^((12/5)*(1-alpha))*log(T)^9) uniformly on[1/2,1].

For alpha>=1/2, Euler-product zero-freeness in Re(s)>1 puts every Ingham positive-height zero within beta<=1. Hence every such zero lies in Huxley’s closed both-sign rectangle: N_I(alpha,T)<=N_H(alpha,T). No doubling or endpoint subtraction is required for this upper bound.
Use the eventual zero-free input with fixed A=16. Then b+B/A=12/5+9/16=237/80 and 1-1/(b+B/A)=157/237.
Set theta=2/3. Its strict margin above the required lower endpoint is 2/3-157/237=1/237>0, while theta<1.
Ingham Theorem1 therefore gives the full pi(x+x^(2/3))-pi(x)~x^(2/3)/log(x) on the real ray as x→∞.
Starting at x=n^3, define x_0=x and x_(j+1)=x_j+x_j^(2/3) for j=0,1,2. Then x_3=x+3*x^(2/3)+2*x^(1/3)+O(1).
(n+1)^3=x+3*x^(2/3)+3*x^(1/3)+1, so the remaining length is x^(1/3)+O(1)>0 eventually; its prime count is O(x^(1/3))=O(n).
The three adjacent half-open pi differences telescope and sum to a quantity asymptotic to 3*x^(2/3)/log(x)=n^2/log(n). The omitted O(n) prime-count remainder is negligible because log(n)/n→0.

For arbitrary real n, converting pi((n+1)^3)-pi(n^3) to the strictly open interval removes at most the upper endpoint prime, hence changes the count by at most1. No lower endpoint correction is needed because pi(n^3) already excludes it from the difference.
